notes: All twelve pages are Annex D (informative): tail of D.10 (bit filler examples), D.11 Character sets, D.12 COBOL-WORDS directive, D.13 Collating sequences, and the head of D.14 Culturally-specific / culturally-adaptable applications. NO general-format or syntax-skeleton FIGURE appears on any page in this batch - there is no bracket, brace, choice-indicator bar, ellipsis-delimiter or underlined required word anywhere in the range (scripts/spec/page_workunit.py likewise reported '0 with figure content' for all twelve). The priority defect class therefore has no instances here; that is a negative result, not an omission. What the pages do carry is prose plus fixed-form COBOL code fragments, which were compared line by line against the 300 dpi render; the two implicit-filler examples on p1102 were re-cropped and zoomed at ~3x to confirm the transcription reproduces ISO's own inconsistency verbatim ('USAGE BIT PIC 1(5).' in the first example versus 'USAGE BIT PIC(6).' - no '1' - in the second). Other ISO-side oddities faithfully preserved by the markdown and deliberately NOT reported as defects: 'CURRENCY-SIGN IS' hyphenated on p1113, 'USAGE DISPLAY PIC N(80)' on p1113, 'Features in this Working Draft International Standard' on p1112, and the ungrammatical 'This can be useful when a change of compiler that includes new reserved words that conflict with existing code.' on p1106. Paragraphs split by the p1102/p1103 and p1112/p1113 page breaks are joined at the end of the earlier page's slice, which is the transcription's normal reflow convention. The only defects found are heading-level, and they are the same systemic promotion pattern already ledgered for the adjacent batch p1114-p1125.

findings.why_it_matters: Sibling clauses at the same numeric depth are transcribed at different markdown heading levels, so the derived outline mis-parents them: D.11.2/.3/.4 render as peers of D.11 rather than children of it, and D.13.3.2/.3/.4 as peers of D.13.3 rather than children. Anything that reconstructs clause structure from heading level - a generated table of contents, anchor/citation depth, a section-scoped search over the spec - reads the annex hierarchy wrongly, and D.12.1 'General' in particular becomes indistinguishable in level from the clause D.12 it belongs to. The pattern across the file is that only the FIRST subclause under a parent keeps its correct level and every later sibling is promoted to '##'; the adjacent batch reported the identical defect for D.14.3.2.3 onward.
findings.suggested_repair: Derive the heading level from the clause-number depth rather than from position in the file: D.11.2 / D.11.3 / D.11.4 -> '###' (matching '### D.11.1'); D.12.1 / D.12.2 / D.12.3 / D.12.4 / D.12.5 -> '###' (under '## D.12'); D.13.2 / D.13.3 / D.13.4 / D.13.5 -> '###' (matching '### D.13.1'); D.13.3.2 / D.13.3.3 / D.13.3.4 -> '####' (matching '### D.13.3.1' once D.13.3 itself is at '###'). Leave the heading text and the <a id="..."> anchors untouched - only the '#' count changes.

findings.why_it_matters: This is the sharpest instance of the promotion pattern in the batch: D.14.2.3 is a third-level subclause whose own two immediate siblings are correctly at '####', yet it is emitted at '##' - the same level as the top-level clause D.14 - so an outline built from the markdown shows D.14.2.3 leaving D.14.2 and standing beside D.14, and D.14.3 leaving D.14 entirely. Because D.14.2.1/.2 ARE correct here, the inconsistency is internal to one page pair and cannot be explained away as a uniform flattening convention. It also directly contradicts the nesting the standard's own numbering states.
findings.suggested_repair: '## D.14.2.3 Class test for characters in a particular alphabet.' -> '#### D.14.2.3 ...' (matching D.14.2.1 / D.14.2.2), and '## D.14.3 Culturally-adaptable applications' -> '### D.14.3 ...' (matching D.14.1 / D.14.2); '### D.14.3.1 General' (:44777) is then correct as-is at '####'... i.e. once D.14.3 is at '###', promote D.14.3.1 to '####' so the pair stays one level apart.
